title: Matthew 9:14–17
context: John’s disciples ask why they and the Pharisees fast while Jesus’ disciples do not. Jesus answers with wedding joy, a coming removal of the bridegroom, and twin images of new cloth and new wine—kingdom life that cannot be patched onto unreformed forms.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What earlier interpreters on each side wrote about Matthew 9:14–17.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: The children of the bride chamber - The companions of the bridegroom. Mourn - Mourning and fasting usually go together. As if he had said, While I am with them, it is a festival time, a season of rejoicing, not mourning. But after I am gone, all my disciples likewise shall be in fastings often.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 9:14–17)

reformed.quote: Luke represents the Pharisees as speaking: Mark appears to connect both. And, indeed, there is no room to doubt that the Pharisees maliciously endeavored, by this stratagem, to draw the disciples of John to their party, and to produce a quarrel between them and the disciples of Christ.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 9:14–17)

verses.text: Then John’s disciples came to him, saying, “Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples don’t fast?”
verses.arminianNotes:
A sincere puzzle from John’s circle: disciplined fasting marks their piety and the Pharisees’, yet Jesus’ disciples feast. Comparison can breed confusion even among the serious.

Honest questions are welcome. Grace does not mock seekers. Still, the question assumes that spiritual vitality is measured by shared austerity rather than by the Bridegroom’s presence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Disciples of the forerunner press the Messiah with a piety comparison. Fasting is not condemned; timing and meaning are.

Revelation progresses. What fit John’s waiting season is not the full measure of life with the Bridegroom present. Scripture interprets piety under Christ’s lordship, not peer pressure.

verses.text: Jesus said to them, “Can the friends of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wedding imagery: Jesus is Bridegroom; disciples are guests. Mourning-fasts clash with His presence. Yet He foretells removal—cross-shaped absence—and then fasting will fit.

Classical Arminians hear both joy and warning. Stay near the Bridegroom while He offers Himself; do not invent grief He has not appointed. When He is “taken away,” disciplined longing has its place. Jesus, not ritual calendars, sets the meaning of fasting.
verses.reformedNotes:
Messianic self-claim: Bridegroom of God’s people. Presence defines the feast; “taken away” quietly points to the passion under the Father’s plan.

The stage of redemptive history governs the practice of fasting. The church will fast in the overlap of ages, but never as if the Bridegroom failed. Joy and sorrow both submit to His timeline.
verses.keyContrast: Both center fasting on Jesus’ presence and coming absence. Arminians often emphasize responsive discipleship that rejoices or fasts as He appoints; Reformed readers often emphasize the sovereign schedule of redemption that defines those seasons.

verses.text: No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment; for the patch would tear away from the garment, and a worse hole is made.
verses.arminianNotes:
New cloth on old cloth worsens the tear. Kingdom newness cannot be a patch on unreformed religion.

Do not reduce Jesus to an upgrade for prideful systems. He calls for new life—repentance and faith—not cosmetic religion. Hearers remain responsible to receive the new rather than force it onto the old.
verses.reformedNotes:
The parable exposes the incompatibility of old and new. Messiah’s work is not a repair kit for self-made righteousness.

God brings a new covenant reality in Christ. Trying to stitch gospel wine onto works-garments only deepens the rip.

verses.text: Neither do people put new wine into old wineskins, or else the skins would burst, and the wine be spilled, and the skins ruined. No, they put new wine into fresh wineskins, and both are preserved.”
verses.arminianNotes:
New wine needs fresh skins—or both are lost. Jesus preserves what is truly new by fitting forms to new life.

Receive the gospel’s newness; let structures serve life in Christ. Preservation is the goal—both wine and skins—when hearts yield to the Bridegroom’s way.
verses.reformedNotes:
New wine is the kingdom inaugurated in Christ; fresh skins are the people and patterns God appoints for it.

God preserves His work. The point is not novelty for its own sake but fidelity to what the Father gives in the Son—life that old wineskins of unbelief cannot contain.
verses.keyContrast: Both reject forcing Jesus into unreformed religion. Arminians emphasize willing reception of new life; Reformed readers underline God’s provision of new covenant reality that unbelief’s forms cannot hold.
